tldr: In PixelGoal navigation—where a robot navigates simply by specifying a single target point on a camera image—the authors proposed "OccPlanner." It integrates 3D occupancy automatically generated from monocular video and uses a diffusion model to generate safe, continuous trajectories. In long-range, obstacle-rich unseen environments, it dramatically boosts success rates from around 21% with conventional methods to approximately 72%.
hero_caption: Overall view of OccPlanner and L3ROcc. The top row shows L3ROcc, which automatically generates visibility-aware 3D occupancy ground-truth data from monocular RGB video. The bottom row shows OccPlanner, which uses the local 3D geometry learned from that data, RGB-D history, and image goals to generate collision-free, safe trajectories via a diffusion model.
overview:
PixelGoal navigation, where an operator simply taps a target pixel on the robot's camera view to say "go here," is exceptionally intuitive because it requires no prior global maps or GPS coordinates. However, a single point on an image tells you neither the metric distance to the destination nor the traversability of the path around obstacles. Conventional PixelGoal approaches attempt to map image features directly to actions, causing them to collide in cluttered areas with furniture and obstacles or lose track of distant goals.

To solve this, the authors propose "OccPlanner," a diffusion planner that predicts local 3D occupancy around the robot and uses it to condition smooth, continuous trajectories. A major bottleneck here is how to collect large amounts of 3D occupancy supervision data. The authors address this by developing "L3ROcc," an automated pipeline that performs 3D geometric reconstruction and line-of-sight ray tracing on monocular RGB navigation videos to produce voxel-level labels.

In evaluations, closed-loop simulation runs were conducted across 60 unseen scenes totaling 6,000 episodes. In the long-range setting of 5–8 m, existing diffusion planner NavDP achieved a success rate of 20.81%, while OccPlanner reached 71.55% (and up to 86.20% in heavily cluttered scenes), demonstrating an overwhelming advantage. Furthermore, real-world experiments on a Unitree Go2 quadruped robot confirmed both zero-shot transfer from simulation and domain adaptability through real-world data.
contributions: Proposed OccPlanner, a diffusion planner that grounds image-space target points into a robot-centric 3D space and generates collision-free continuous trajectories conditioned on local 3D occupancy features.
Introduced a two-stage goal conditioning mechanism that progressively fuses temporal visual context and 3D occupancy features, boosting accuracy with an auxiliary 3D ego-goal prediction task.

Developed L3ROcc, a data pipeline that performs geometric reconstruction and ray-marching on monocular RGB navigation videos to automatically generate 3D occupancy annotations distinguishing visible, free, and unknown space.

sections.heading: Why Is Just Tapping the Screen to Navigate So Hard?
sections.summary: PixelGoal navigation, which sets a single point in an image as the destination, is practical, but the lack of distance and traversability information makes collision avoidance difficult. This work breaks through that barrier by fusing local 3D occupancy prediction with diffusion models, backed by an automated pipeline that generates training data from monocular video.
sections.details:
For autonomous mobile robots to be useful in the real world, they must generate collision-free, smooth motions in unseen environments from their camera view and goal instructions. While targets can be specified in various formats such as coordinates (PointGoal) or natural language (VLN), PixelGoal navigation—pointing directly to a visible pixel on the current camera view—offers the huge advantage of requiring no prior map creation.

However, this approach faces fundamental challenges. The specified pixel itself contains neither metric depth information nor traversability along the path to reach it. Consequently, the planner must simultaneously infer where the target lies in 3D space and how to avoid surrounding obstacles.

Existing PixelGoal methods (such as PixNav) learn policies directly conditioned on image features, or predict traversable pixels and back-project them into 3D waypoints. In recent local planners, diffusion models have also gained traction for generating diverse trajectories. Nonetheless, these methods remain detached from explicit 3D occupancy reasoning (identifying which regions of space are occupied by objects), making safe navigation through cluttered obstacle fields difficult.

This paper proposes OccPlanner, which grounds pixel goals in a robot-centric 3D space and generates trajectories with a diffusion model based on learned local 3D occupancy features. Moreover, the authors develop L3ROcc to automatically generate the required 3D occupancy annotations in a self-supervised manner from monocular RGB navigation videos, enabling large-scale data supply.

captions.F2: The L3ROcc data generation pipeline. Taking monocular RGB video as input, it uses the geometric foundation model $\pi^3$ to estimate 3D point clouds and camera trajectories. After scale recovery and transformation into the robot frame, voxel-space ray-marching generates local 3D occupancy supervision that cleanly distinguishes visible, free, and unknown space.

sections.heading: From Mapless Navigation to Diffusion Models: What Sets This Work Apart?
sections.summary: This study sits at the intersection of four research areas: navigation goal representations, PixelGoal local planning, monocular 3D reconstruction and occupancy, and diffusion-based trajectory planning. OccPlanner introduces a novel approach by bridging image goals to explicit 3D spatial awareness and continuous trajectory generation.
sections.details:
Prior work related to this paper can be organized into four broad categories:

- Navigation representations and goal settings: Navigation methods using reinforcement learning or imitation learning have explored global maps, topological maps (representing connectivity via nodes and edges), or learning mobility priors from past navigational experience (such as GNM and ViNT). Goal specifications span coordinates, object categories, and natural language instructions, but PixelGoal is the most intuitive setting while demanding strong geometric grounding to translate into executable actions.

- PixelGoal navigation and local planners: Methods like PixNav learn policies directly conditioned on image targets, and Goal2Pixel predicts traversable pixels from language and converts them to 3D waypoints. Conversely, local planners such as iPlanner and ViPlanner generate continuous trajectories from depth images and metric goals. OccPlanner bridges these domains by grounding image targets into the robot-centric 3D frame and producing continuous trajectories from local 3D occupancy.

- Monocular 3D reconstruction and occupancy estimation: Recent models like DUSt3R and $\pi^3$ can accurately reconstruct 3D geometry and camera poses directly from multi-view monocular camera images. In autonomous driving, voxel representations like Occ3D take line-of-sight occlusion into account. L3ROcc combines these techniques to build local occupancy supervision for navigation from monocular video.

- Diffusion models for trajectory planning: Applying diffusion models successful in image generation (such as Diffusion Policy) to robot action and trajectory generation is gaining momentum (e.g., NavDP and LoGoPlanner). OccPlanner distinguishes itself by carefully aligning image goals and predicted occupancy features across two stages, rather than simply denoising trajectories from raw past observations.

sections.heading: L3ROcc: Automatically Labeling Free Space and Obstacles in 3D from Monocular RGB Video
sections.summary: Supervising 3D occupancy requires massive amounts of labels, but expensive LiDAR or manual annotations are costly. L3ROcc was developed to perform 3D geometric reconstruction and ray-marching on monocular RGB navigation videos, automatically generating visibility-aware occupancy annotations from the robot's perspective.
sections.details:
For a robot to understand the surrounding 3D space, 3D occupancy supervision data is essential. However, collecting this in the real world outside simulators is challenging. L3ROcc solves this by automatically generating labels purely from navigation videos recorded with standard monocular cameras.

- 3.1 Overview: L3ROcc takes monocular video, reconstructs scene point clouds and camera trajectories using the recent geometric foundation model $\pi^3$, recovers metric real-world scale, transforms geometry into the robot frame at each timestep, and performs voxelization and visibility determination to generate temporally consistent occupancy.

- 3.2 RGB geometric reconstruction: Sampled video frames are fed into $\pi^3$, filtering out low-confidence points and depth-edge artifacts to yield a clean global point cloud $\mathcal{P}^g$. For camera trajectories, translations are interpolated with splines and rotations with spherical linear interpolation (SLERP) of quaternions, creating a dense pose sequence for all video frames. Camera sight rays are also constructed from the initial viewpoint.

- 3.3 Scale recovery and alignment to the robot frame: Monocular reconstruction inherently carries scale ambiguity. When reference camera poses are available, absolute scale is determined via trajectory alignment; if unavailable, a metric depth model is leveraged to match real-world scale. The point cloud and viewing rays are then rotated and translated into the robot base frame.

- 3.4 Visibility-aware local occupancy generation: This is a crucial design choice. Simply binning point clouds into voxels treats unobserved areas behind obstacles as free space. To prevent this, ray-marching is performed along viewing rays in voxel space. The first voxel hit by a ray is marked as "occupied," voxels before it as "observed free," and voxels behind it as "unknown." This produces realistic, consistent 3D training data for the robot.

captions.F3: Qualitative results of local occupancy generated by L3ROcc. Against the input RGB video in the top row, the bottom row demonstrates that surrounding 3D geometry (furniture, walls, hallways) and the navigation trajectory (blue line) are smoothly and consistently reconstructed over time without temporal breakdown.

sections.heading: OccPlanner Architecture: Guiding Smooth Trajectories with Occupancy and Two-Stage Attention
sections.summary: OccPlanner comprises an RGB-D geometric encoder, a local 3D occupancy prediction branch, and a trajectory generation branch that integrates the goal and environment. It cross-attends the image goal with visual context and near-ground occupancy in two stages, using a diffusion model to generate safe continuous trajectories.
sections.details:
OccPlanner takes the recent RGB-D observation history and an image goal specification to output 24 future waypoints for the robot to track. The architecture operates through three primary branches.

- 4.2 Shared RGB-D geometric encoder: Past 8 frames of RGB and depth images serve as inputs. RGB is encoded by DINOv2 and depth by Depth Anything V2 (ViT-S), concatenated per patch. Passing these through the spatio-temporal attention blocks of $\pi^3$ extracts geometric features $\mathbf{H}$ capturing per-frame local geometry and temporal context. It also prepares a spatio-temporal context $\mathbf{U}_{\mathrm{ctx}}$ compressing recent observations and past history.

- 4.3 Occupancy prediction branch: From the latest geometric features, 2D features are lifted to 3D space and passed through a 3D convolutional decoder to predict 3D occupancy voxels around the robot. Because obstacles right near the floor are most critical for collision avoidance, a near-ground slice is extracted from the predicted features into a 2D feature map and compressed into compact occupancy tokens $\mathbf{Z}_{\mathrm{occ}}$ via cross-attention with learnable queries.

- 4.4 Two-stage goal conditioning mechanism: This is the core architectural innovation. The specified pixel coordinates $(u, v)$ are first embedded with multi-frequency Fourier features to form a goal token $\mathbf{z}_g$. Instead of simple concatenation, this token undergoes cross-attention with the temporal context in Stage 1, followed by cross-attention with occupancy tokens in Stage 2. The resulting ego-goal representation $\mathbf{z}_e$ is simultaneously trained on an auxiliary task predicting the 3D egocentric goal position $\mathbf{g}_{\mathrm{ego}}$, grounding where the target lies in 3D relative to the robot.

- 4.5 Diffusion-based trajectory planning: Trajectory generation adopts the Diffusion Policy framework. A goal-aware state token, spatio-temporal context, ego-goal representation, and occupancy tokens are packed into conditioning context $\mathbf{C}_\ell$. A Transformer decoder performs 10 denoising steps from noisy action sequences to reconstruct a smooth, collision-free future action trajectory $\hat{\mathbf{A}}_0$.

- 4.6 Training loss functions: The entire model is trained end-to-end with a combined loss: the occupancy prediction loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{occ}}$, the diffusion model noise-prediction MSE loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{diff}}$, and the auxiliary 3D goal regression loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ego}}$.

captions.F4: Overall architecture of OccPlanner. Geometric features are extracted from input RGB-D, and the occupancy branch handles 3D occupancy prediction and near-ground tokenization. In the trajectory branch, the pixel goal is integrated in two stages with context and occupancy, allowing the diffusion planner to generate smooth action trajectories.

sections.heading: Over 80% Success Rate in Unseen Cluttered Rooms: Simulation and Real-World Experiments
sections.summary: Evaluated across 60 unseen scenes and 6,000 episodes in the InternScenes simulator, OccPlanner dramatically improved the long-range success rate from NavDP's ~21% to ~72%. Real-world experiments on a Unitree Go2 and detailed ablation studies confirm the superiority of progressively fusing occupancy.
sections.details:
The authors conducted comprehensive evaluations across both simulation and physical robot platforms.

- 5.1 Experimental setup: Training utilized over 200,000 trajectories from the InternData-N1 simulation dataset, automatically labeled using L3ROcc. OccPlanner takes 8 input frames ($224\times 224$) and outputs 24-step waypoints, trained across 4 NVIDIA H100 GPUs for roughly 48 hours.

- 5.2 Simulation evaluation: Closed-loop evaluations were carried out across 60 unseen InternScenes (20 residential, 20 commercial, 10 cluttered-simple, 10 cluttered-hard) over 6,000 episodes spanning short-range (3–5 m) and long-range (5–8 m) settings. An episode succeeds if the robot stops within 0.5 m of the goal. OccPlanner was compared against NavDP (adapted for pixel goals) and the image-based reinforcement learning baseline PixNav.

- Quantitative findings: In the long-range (5–8 m) setting, OccPlanner demonstrated outstanding performance. Success rates rose from NavDP's 24.98% to 69.90% in residential scenes, and from 19.07% to 45.17% in commercial scenes. Most remarkably, in narrow and obstacle-heavy environments, success jumped from 19.43% to 86.20% in cluttered-simple and from 19.77% to 84.92% in cluttered-hard—a massive gain exceeding 65 percentage points. PixNav failed almost entirely over long distances (success rates below a few percent).

- 5.3 Physical robot experiments: Open-loop evaluation was conducted using a Unitree Go2 quadruped robot in a cluttered office with cardboard boxes, chairs, and narrow passages. While the model trained purely on simulation exhibited zero-shot obstacle avoidance for coarse structures, fine-tuning on 829 real-world videos labeled with L3ROcc sharpened predicted obstacle boundaries and yielded smooth trajectories that neatly circumvented furniture.

- 5.4 Ablation analysis: In cluttered environments, the 3D ego-goal auxiliary task pushed success rates up by 15–20 percentage points. Furthermore, using two-stage attention rather than simple feature concatenation boosted hard-cluttered success from 75.55% to 84.92%. Interestingly, baseline models with superior offline trajectory errors (FDE) often performed worse in online success rates, highlighting the vital importance of closed-loop deployment evaluations.

captions.F5: Qualitative results in simulation. In cluttered, commercial, and residential environments, OccPlanner generates safe, collision-free trajectories (red lines) that weave through the open areas of the predicted occupancy toward the image goal (red point).
captions.F6: Real-world open-loop evaluation comparison on the Unitree Go2. Compared to the zero-shot model (trained only on simulation, top row), the real-world fine-tuned model (bottom row) predicts denser, more accurate occupancy around office boxes and chairs, enabling safe trajectory forecasts even in tight corridors.

sections.heading: Summary and Next Steps: Paving the Way for Real-World Closed-Loop Navigation
sections.summary: OccPlanner combines intuitive point-and-click goals on camera images with safe 3D autonomous mobility, enabled by the automated L3ROcc data engine. Outperforming existing methods in long-range and cluttered environments, future work aims toward full closed-loop real-world autonomy and handling dynamic obstacles.
sections.details:
This work opens up a practical framework allowing robots to navigate safely without pre-built maps simply by indicating a target point on an image. The breakthrough stems from uniting L3ROcc—a data engine that automatically generates high-quality 3D occupancy annotations from monocular video—with OccPlanner, which meticulously embeds 3D geometric awareness and goal grounding into diffusion trajectory planning.

Large-scale simulation experiments proved the indispensable role of explicit occupancy reasoning, yielding decisive advantages over baselines in cluttered, furniture-dense environments.

Currently, real-world evaluations remain open-loop tests on recorded data within static indoor scenes. Looking ahead, the authors highlight real-time closed-loop autonomous navigation on physical hardware, extending predictions to dynamic obstacles like moving pedestrians, and achieving long-range navigation toward distant, occluded destinations.

takeaways: Even when targeting a 2D pixel on an image, internally predicting and reasoning over explicit 3D occupancy voxels is remarkably effective for avoiding collisions in complex environments.

Combining monocular RGB navigation videos with modern geometric foundation models (like $\pi^3$) and ray-marching makes it possible to mass-produce high-quality 3D occupancy supervision without expensive sensors.
When providing occupancy features to the planner, progressively interacting temporal context and occupancy via goal representations—rather than raw feature concatenation—is critical for performance.
Offline trajectory error metrics (such as FDE) do not always correlate with online navigation success rates, underscoring the absolute necessity of closed-loop behavioral evaluations.
limitations: Real-world robot experiments are currently limited to open-loop trajectory predictions on recorded datasets; real-time closed-loop navigation on physical hardware has yet to be demonstrated.
The framework does not model motion forecasts for dynamic obstacles (e.g., pedestrians or carts), assuming a static indoor environment.

The target location must be visible in the agent's initial camera view (free from full occlusion); the model cannot independently conduct exploratory navigation to goals hidden behind walls or outside the field of view.
